chapters.title: Chapter 1: What Implied Volatility Actually Means

lessons.title: Reading IV on a Live Nifty Option Chain

children.text: From Theory to the Screen: What You Are Actually Looking At

Three lessons of theory now meet a screen full of numbers. There are two main places to read a live Nifty option chain. NSE's own website (nseindia.com) is free, official, and the ultimate source of truth, but it refreshes periodically rather than tick by tick. Broker and analytics terminals, such as Zerodha Kite with its Sensibull integration, Upstox Pro, Angel One, or a dedicated tool like Opstra, compute and refresh IV in close to real time, using solvers built on the same Newton-Raphson idea from Lesson 2, running silently in the background every time a price ticks.
Anatomy of an Option Chain Row

Almost every chain, NSE's or a broker's, lays out the same way: call-side data on the left, the strike price in the middle, put-side data on the right, and the row nearest the current spot price (the ATM strike) usually shaded. A typical row runs Call OI, Call LTP, Call IV, Strike, Put IV, Put LTP, Put OI. Here is a sample snapshot to practice reading, continuing the same Nifty setup from Lessons 2 and 3: spot at 24,800, 7 calendar days to weekly expiry.

body.caption: Illustrative Nifty weekly option chain snapshot (Spot: 24,800, 7 days to expiry)

children.text: Read it the way a desk would. Find the ATM strike first: 24,800, shaded in the table. Its Call IV and Put IV sit almost exactly together at 10.85%, exactly what Lesson 3's put-call parity argument predicts. Now scan up and down the strikes. IV is not flat. It climbs to 14.5 to 14.6% at the 24,200 strike and drifts down to roughly 9.1 to 9.5% by 25,200 and 25,400. That steady decline from low strikes to high strikes is a real, common shape on index option chains, and it has a name: the volatility skew, which is the entire subject of the next chapter. For now, just notice it is there.

body.text: The put side of a strike below spot and the call side of a strike above spot are the out-of-the-money (OTM) leg at that strike, and OTM legs almost always trade more actively than their in-the-money counterpart at the same strike. When call and put IV disagree at a strike, lean on the OTM side's IV as the more liquid, more trustworthy reading; that habit becomes essential once you start reading skew properly in Chapter 2.

children.text: Now look at the 25,400 row. Its Call IV of 6.20% breaks the pattern completely, a sudden drop when every neighboring strike is declining gently. Look at what sits next to it: zero volume today and a last traded price that is three hours stale. This is exactly the failure mode from Lesson 2's Priya scenario, showing up live on a real-looking chain. The put side of that same strike, 9.10%, looks perfectly consistent with the trend and comes with real volume behind it. The call side's number is not a market opinion. It is a stale-price artefact.
The Expiry-Level IV Number: What the Summary Tile Means

Most broker and analytics terminals also show a single headline number near the top of the chain, something like "IV: 10.9%" for the expiry you are viewing. This is usually the ATM straddle's implied volatility, or a small weighted average of the strikes nearest the money, and it is what people casually mean when they say "Nifty's IV is around 11% this week." It is worth keeping this distinct from India VIX, covered in Lesson 1: VIX is NSE's own separate calculation, aggregated across a wider strip of strikes and blended across the near and next expiry to represent a fixed 30-calendar-day expectation. The expiry-tile IV on your broker's screen and India VIX are related, often close in value, but they are not computed the same way and will not always match to the decimal.

body.label: Two numbers people both call "the IV", and how they differ
body.value: Expiry-tile IV (~10.9%) vs India VIX (a separate NSE calculation)
body.context: The expiry tile is usually an ATM/weighted average for the specific expiry you are looking at. India VIX is NSE's own fixed 30-calendar-day expectation, blended across near and next expiry, computed from the full bid-ask order book rather than a single platform's chosen solver.

children.text: A Checklist for Trusting What You See

body.title: Five checks before you trust an IV number on a chain
steps: Check today's volume and open interest on that specific strike, not just that a number is displayed
Check the bid-ask spread width; a wide spread on a thinly traded strike means its IV is shaky
Confirm you are reading the expiry you meant to read; near-week and monthly IV can differ a lot
Compare call IV and put IV at the same strike; a large, unexplained gap flags bad data more often than it flags a real opportunity
Cross-check the strike or expiry-tile IV against the broader index number, such as India VIX for Nifty, to see if what you are looking at seems like a normal read or an outlier

body.title: Spotting the unreliable print
body.question: Looking at the sample chain above, the 25,400 strike shows a Call IV of 6.20%, noticeably lower than every neighboring strike, while its Put IV sits at a normal-looking 9.10%. What should you conclude?
options: The 25,400 call is a genuine, tradeable outlier and should be bought immediately since its IV looks unusually cheap

The 25,400 Call IV is almost certainly unreliable: its last traded price is stale (three hours old) with zero volume today, so 6.20% is a stale-price artefact rather than a real market view; the strike's Put IV and open interest both look normal, which points squarely at the call side as the problem
A call and put at the same strike are never expected to show similar IV, so this is completely unremarkable
The low Call IV means Nifty is now expected to rally sharply past 25,400
body.explanation: The checklist points straight at this one: near-zero volume and a stale multi-hour-old last traded price are the classic signature of an unreliable IV print, exactly as in Lesson 2's Priya scenario. The healthy Put IV and normal open interest at the same strike confirm the strike itself is fine; it is specifically the stale call-side price that is producing a misleading number.

columns.label: NSE website (nseindia.com)
points: Free, official, and the ultimate source of truth for settlement
Refreshes periodically rather than tick by tick, so IV can lag a fast-moving market
Shows raw OI, volume, and LTP for every strike
No account or login needed to check it

columns.label: Broker/analytics terminals (Kite + Sensibull, Upstox Pro, Opstra, and similar)
points: Compute and refresh IV in close to real time as prices tick
Usually highlight the ATM row and often show an expiry-level summary IV tile
Layer on extras like OI change, PCR, and payoff visualizers
Require a broker account or subscription; each platform's solver can show slightly different IV for the same strike, since the exact price and inputs it feeds the solver can differ, as in Lesson 2

body.text: An option chain is not a wall of numbers to skim. It is dozens of small IV calculations happening at once, one per strike, each only as trustworthy as the price and liquidity sitting behind it. Reading a chain well starts with knowing which numbers to trust before you try to figure out what they mean.

points: NSE's own site is the official source of option chain data but updates periodically; broker and analytics terminals (Kite + Sensibull, Upstox Pro, Opstra, and similar) compute and refresh IV closer to real time.
A standard chain row runs Call OI, Call LTP, Call IV, Strike, Put IV, Put LTP, Put OI, with the ATM row usually shaded.
Reading down a live chain, IV is rarely flat across strikes: it typically declines from low strikes to high strikes on index options, a preview of the volatility skew covered in the next chapter.
A single expiry-level IV number shown on most terminals is usually an ATM or weighted average, a different calculation from India VIX, even though both get called "the IV" in everyday conversation.

Before trusting any IV figure on a chain, check today's volume and OI, the bid-ask width, that call and put IV at the same strike are close, and that you are reading the expiry you actually meant to read.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. The option chain snapshot is a hypothetical, illustrative table built to continue the Nifty example from Lessons 2 and 3, not a live NSE or broker data feed. Real chains change every second markets are open. Always check the live chain on NSE or your broker's terminal (such as Zerodha Kite, Sensibull, Upstox Pro, or Opstra) before trading, and consult a SEBI-registered advisor for personalised advice.
